one_liner: Heap-free, fixed-capacity STL-style containers (vector, map, unordered_map) for embedded C++03+; no maintained speed claim against std.
what_it_does: ETL gives STL-like containers whose maximum size is a template parameter (etl::vector<T,N>, etl::map<K,V,N>, etl::unordered_map<K,V,N,BUCKETS>), with all storage inside the object, so the heap is never touched. Each has a size-erased base (ivector, imap, iunordered_map) for passing containers of different capacities through one interface. The API mirrors the std containers closely but they are distinct types, and overflow is an error condition rather than growth.
how_it_is_fast: There is no algorithmic trick; any speed edge comes from never calling malloc/free. Node containers (map, unordered_map) draw nodes from an embedded etl::pool: an intrusive free list threaded through unused slots with lazy initialisation, so allocate and release are O(1) pointer pops. etl::unordered_map is separate chaining over intrusive singly linked buckets indexed by hash % bucket_count with no rehashing; etl::map is an AVL-style balanced binary tree (per-node balance field) on the same pool. etl::hash<uint64_t> on a 64-bit target is the identity function.
when_to_use: Firmware or RTOS code where dynamic allocation is banned or must be bounded, and the worst-case element count is known at build time.
Hard real-time paths that need insert/erase without allocator latency spikes (node pool allocate/release is O(1)).
Toolchains stuck on C++03 or without a usable STL (Keil, IAR, TI, avr-gcc, Arduino) where you still want map/unordered_map/vector semantics.
Small, bounded lookup tables with integer keys where a statically sized hash map or AVL map is enough.
when_not_to_use: Host or server code chasing throughput: chained buckets plus a modulo per lookup are not competitive with open-addressing tables; nothing shows ETL beating a modern std::unordered_map replacement.

Unknown or highly variable sizes: capacity cannot grow, and an unordered_map<K,V,N> reserves N nodes plus N buckets up front (on 64-bit about 16 bytes per bucket and a link pointer per node, used or not).

Workloads that erase keys in descending order or repeatedly erase the highest-index occupied bucket: each such erase rescans buckets from first to last (O(bucket range)), so with identity-hashed sequential keys a reverse-order erase is quadratic.
Keys that share low-order bits with a fixed bucket count (e.g. multiples of the bucket count) under the identity integer hash: there is no rehash, so they pile into one chain.

integration.dependencies: none (optionally uses the STL unless ETL_NO_STL is defined; chrono and print need user-supplied platform hooks)
integration.min_toolchain: C++03 (C++98 badge); CI on GCC and Clang for C++11 through C++26, MSVC; README says tested with VS2022, GCC 12, Clang 14; CMake 3.10+ for the INTERFACE target
integration.platforms: any (bare metal, RTOS, desktop); also Arduino, Zephyr, PlatformIO, Conan packages
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the container and pool code read has no internal synchronisation
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: std-like member names, but capacity is a template parameter, the types are not std types, there is no allocator parameter, and growth past capacity is an error

gotchas: Overflow checking depends on macros: etl::vector::push_back is unchecked unless ETL_CHECK_PUSH_POP is defined (the vector doc implies asserts or exceptions suffice), and with no ETL_THROW_EXCEPTIONS/ETL_LOG_ERRORS in an NDEBUG build ETL_ASSERT is a no-op, so inserting into a full unordered_map gets a null node from the pool and dereferences it.
unordered_map::erase rescans buckets from first to last whenever the erased node sits in the current last bucket; the shipped harness erases in ascending order and never hits this path.

The only timing harness (test/Performance/unordered_map, Dec 2016, VS2015 v140 project) includes ../../../../src/unordered_map.h and src/ipool.h; the repo has no src/ directory now (code is in include/etl), so it does not build against the current tree without edits.

That harness favours ETL by construction: identity etl::hash with sequential keys 0..N-1 and N buckets gives one key per bucket walked in memory order, the ETL map is a pre-sized 10M-capacity global while std::unordered_map rehashes as it grows in round 1, the std loop runs first in the same process, and each container is timed once.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick ETL over EASTL's fixed containers or sfl-library's static_vector when you need the whole fixed-capacity family (vector, map, unordered_map, strings, pools) with zero heap fallback and C++03 support on embedded compilers; pick EASTL (published std comparisons) or ankerl::svector / sfl small_vector when you want inline storage that can still spill to the heap, and fast_vector or veque when raw std::vector throughput is the goal.
verified_claims_summary: No speed claim in the README or docs, but GitHub issue #13 holds first-party numbers from the maintainer (Dec 31, 2016; Intel i7 3.40 GHz, Windows 10 x64, Visual Studio 2015 /O2): 16 rounds of insert-then-erase of N sequential uint64_t->uint16_t keys, std::unordered_map vs etl::unordered_map, 26 vs 4 ms at 10k, 437 vs 41 ms at 100k, 6,386 vs 420 ms at 1M and 88,020 vs 4,096 ms at 10M (about 21x, derived from page data), measured on the then-new pool before its Feb 2017 release, apparently with the in-repo harness (committed the same day, same 16 rounds). Two days earlier a third party (bkaradzic, bx handle_bench) had found ETL the slowest map (ETL 9,690 vs STL 3,573 vs TinySTL 4,534, unitless), which the maintainer traced to the old bitset pool and fixed; no one has re-measured since.
status_note: Actively maintained (v20.49.0, last commit 2026-10-04, 3.1k stars, vendored under 3rdparty in the Qt for MCUs 2.1 automotive demo) and MIT-licensed header-only, so copyable; the 2016 issue #13 numbers make the unordered_map claim first-party (tier C at best: CPU model not given, pre-release code, stale harness with an identity-hash best case), while vector and map have no measurement at all.
